papers.headline: Psilocybin and ketamine make mice slower but more accurate decision-makers
papers.original_title: Psychedelics shift decision strategies and reconfigure orbitofrontal dynamics
papers.reason: Psilocybin and ketamine shift mice toward sensory-guided decision strategies and reconfigure orbitofrontal dynamics.
papers.summary:
Drugs like psilocybin (the active compound in 'magic mushrooms') and ketamine are being studied as fast-acting treatments for mental health conditions, but it is unclear how they change the way the brain makes choices. The researchers trained mice on a task where the animals responded at their own pace to judge a sensory signal. The task was designed to separate two strategies: relying on a built-in preference (bias) versus actually using the sensory information. The mice then received a single dose of psilocybin or ketamine.

On either drug, mice took longer to decide but chose correctly more often. Mathematical models of the behaviour suggested the mice were waiting for more evidence before committing to a choice, and were spending more time in a 'paying attention to the stimulus' mode rather than a bias-driven mode. Mapping a marker of recent neural activity across the whole brain showed the drugs altered networks used in the task, including the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), a frontal region involved in decisions. Recording OFC neurons showed they still responded to task events, but the timing of their activity and how they fired together had changed.
papers.why_it_matters: The study offers a link between what these drugs do to behaviour and what they do to brain circuits, suggesting they push decisions to depend more on incoming sensory evidence. This could help explain how such drugs affect thinking, which matters as they are tested as therapies.
papers.limitations: This was done in mice after a single, acute dose, so it is unclear how well the results apply to people or to longer-term therapeutic use. The abstract does not establish that the OFC changes cause the behavioural shift.

key_terms.meaning: A model treating a decision as evidence building up over time until it reaches a threshold; a higher threshold means slower but more careful choices.
A statistical method that detects hidden 'states' an animal switches between, such as following the stimulus versus following a habitual bias.
Staining for a protein that neurons make after being active, used to see which brain areas were engaged.
A technique that tracks neuron activity by watching fluorescent signals that change when calcium enters active cells.
A region at the front of the brain involved in evaluating options and making decisions.

papers.headline: Brain ripples in the hippocampus grow while people hold images in short-term memory
papers.original_title: Ramping-up hippocampal ripples and their neocortical coupling support human visual short-term memory
papers.reason: Intracranial recordings show that hippocampal ripples ramp up and couple with neocortex during human visual short-term memory maintenance.
papers.summary:
The hippocampus, a seahorse-shaped structure deep in the brain, is best known for long-term memory. There are growing hints that it also helps us keep visual information in mind for a few seconds, but how it does this has been unclear. The researchers studied hippocampal ripples, which are very short bursts of fast electrical activity thought to accompany the 'replay' of memories. They used electrodes placed inside the brains of human patients (intracranial EEG) while the participants did a task: view a picture of a real-world object, hold it in mind through a delay, then judge whether a test image matched it.

Across the delay, ripples in the hippocampus became steadily more frequent, and this increase was linked to getting the memory test right. Hippocampal ripples also tended to occur at the same moments as ripples in the lateral temporal lobe, a region of the outer brain (neocortex) involved in recognising objects. When ripples in the two areas happened together, the lateral temporal lobe showed signs of re-activating the remembered object's activity pattern. The authors interpret this as the hippocampus and neocortex communicating through linked ripples to keep short-term visual memories alive.
papers.why_it_matters: Ripples have mostly been studied as a way the brain strengthens long-term memories, for example during sleep. This work suggests the same signal may also help hold information over seconds, which changes how researchers think about working memory. It also points to a specific timing mechanism by which deep and outer brain regions might cooperate.
papers.limitations: The abstract does not give the number of participants, and intracranial recordings typically come from patients with a medical condition, which may limit how far results generalise. The findings show ripples are linked to memory success, but the abstract does not establish that ripples cause better memory.

key_terms.meaning: Keeping a picture or visual detail in mind for a few seconds after it disappears.
Brief, high-frequency bursts of electrical activity in the hippocampus, linked to replaying memories.
Recording brain electrical activity with electrodes placed inside the skull, usually in patients being assessed for epilepsy surgery.
A test where you see an item, wait through a delay, then decide whether a new item matches the first.
The outer side part of the brain near the ears, involved in recognising objects and storing knowledge.
When the brain activity pattern seen during viewing an item reappears while it is being remembered.

papers.headline: Satellites catch an Ethiopian volcano releasing record amounts of methane without erupting
papers.original_title: Methane outburst driven by magma–sediment interactions at Fentale Volcano detected by satellite
papers.reason: Satellites detected a methane outburst at a non-erupting volcano, linked to magma intrusion into hydrocarbon-rich sediments.
papers.summary:
Volcanoes normally give off very little methane, yet magma pushing into carbon-rich sedimentary rock is thought to have released huge amounts of greenhouse gas during episodes of sudden climate change in Earth's past. Researchers lacked a modern example of this process. After a very large sheet of magma (a 'mega-dyke') forced its way underground near Fentale Volcano in Ethiopia's rift valley in late 2024 and early 2025, the team used a range of satellites to track gas, heat, ground movement and visible plumes inside the volcano's caldera, even though no lava ever reached the surface.

They estimate Fentale emitted at least about 38 thousand tonnes of methane over roughly three months, about 90% of it in the first month, plus at least 2.9 million tonnes of carbon dioxide over 14 days. The peak methane rate, around 157 tonnes per hour, matched major gas-well blowouts and was roughly 10,000 times higher than rates measured at other volcanoes. The gas release came alongside ground sinking and hot spots in the caldera, followed in February by a collapse about 40 m deep. The authors propose that the magma cracked a sealed rock 'lid' under which methane had built up. They think this methane came from heated, hydrocarbon-rich ancient sediments.
papers.why_it_matters: This appears to be the first satellite detection of methane from a volcano, and it reveals a natural source of sudden methane bursts that is not counted in current methane budgets or volcanic hazard plans. It also offers a small, modern window into how magma meeting sediments may have warmed the planet in the deep past. Large invisible clouds of carbon dioxide and methane in a caldera can also be deadly to people nearby.
papers.limitations: No ground-based gas samples or carbon isotope measurements were taken at Fentale, so the sediment origin of the methane is inferred from regional data and geology. Limited satellite passes mean carbon dioxide totals are likely underestimates, and the burst is tiny compared with yearly human methane emissions.

key_terms.meaning: Magma squeezing into a vertical crack in the crust and cooling there without erupting at the surface.
A large bowl-shaped depression at the top of a volcano, often formed by collapse.
Methane made when buried organic material in sedimentary rock is cooked by heat, as in natural gas fields.
A layer of rock that gas cannot pass through, trapping it underneath until the layer breaks.
Enormous outpourings of magma in Earth's history, some linked to rapid climate change and mass extinctions.
Sinking of the ground surface, here measured from space with radar.

papers.headline: Pacific low-oxygen zone barely changed through the last three ice ages
papers.original_title: Insensitivity of the North Pacific oxygen-deficient zone to recent ice age cycle climate changes
papers.reason: Foraminifera-bound nitrogen isotope records show the North Pacific oxygen-deficient zone stayed stable through glacial–interglacial cycles.
papers.summary:
Off the Pacific coast of Central America lies an oxygen-deficient zone (ODZ), a mid-depth layer of seawater with almost no oxygen. In it, microbes strip usable nitrogen out of the ocean (denitrification). Earlier studies measured nitrogen isotopes in bulk seafloor mud and concluded that this zone shrank during ice ages and grew in warm periods. The researchers tested that idea using a more protected archive: organic nitrogen locked inside the shells of foraminifera (tiny shelled plankton). They analysed two species from a drilling site (ODP Site 1241) at the southern edge of the eastern tropical North Pacific ODZ, covering about the last 265,000 years and three ice-age-to-warm transitions. For direct comparison, they also measured bulk mud back to about 60,000 years ago.

The shell-based record shifted only about 2 per mil and did not track global temperature, ice volume or CO2. For example, values at the peak of the last ice age (about 10.3) were close to those of the late Holocene (about 10.8). The bulk-mud record from the same cores, by contrast, showed ice-age values 3–4 per mil lower. The authors argue the mud signal was distorted by chemical changes after burial or by nitrogen washed in from land. The zone did grow briefly during each of the last three deglaciations, and at times when Earth's orbit strengthened the tropical rain belt at its northern extreme. They suggest this happened because stronger winds drove more upwelling and biological productivity.
papers.why_it_matters: Models disagree about how ocean low-oxygen zones will respond to global warming, and these zones affect nitrogen loss and production of the greenhouse gas nitrous oxide. This record suggests the North Pacific zone may change little with 1–2 °C of warming. Together with older, warmer-era records, it also hints the zone could weaken substantially under stronger warming.
papers.limitations: The record comes mainly from one site at the southern edge of the zone, so the northern part may have behaved differently. The data resolve only changes over thousands of years, not decades. The proposed explanations, either stabilizing feedbacks in the thermocline (the sharp temperature boundary below the warm surface layer) or offsetting iron fertilization in the Southern Ocean, remain untested hypotheses.

key_terms.meaning: A mid-depth ocean region where dissolved oxygen is nearly used up by decaying organic matter.
Microbes converting nitrate into nitrogen gas, removing nitrogen that living things can use. It favours light nitrogen, so the nitrate left behind becomes richer in heavy nitrogen-15.
The ratio of heavy to light nitrogen in organic matter sealed inside plankton shells. Because the shell protects it, this signal is less easily altered than nitrogen in bulk mud.
Chemical and biological changes to sediment after it settles on the seafloor.
The band of rising air and heavy rain near the equator, whose position shifts with seasons and orbital cycles.

papers.headline: More realistic plankton in climate models predict a bigger drop in ocean carbon storage
papers.original_title: Plankton ecological complexity amplifies climate-driven weakening of the ocean biological pump
papers.reason: Earth system modeling suggests that more complex plankton food webs amplify climate-driven weakening of ocean carbon export.
papers.summary:
The ocean's 'biological pump' is the process by which tiny drifting organisms (plankton) take up carbon near the surface, and some of that carbon then sinks into the deep sea when they die or are eaten. Climate change is expected to weaken this pump. The researchers asked whether the predicted size of that weakening depends on how much detail a model includes about plankton and who eats whom.

They used a single Earth system model, a computer simulation of the linked ocean, atmosphere and climate, and ran it with plankton food webs of increasing complexity. The more complex the food web, the larger the climate-driven fall in the amount of carbon moved to the deep ocean. This suggests that simpler models may be underestimating how much the biological pump will weaken in the future.
papers.why_it_matters: The biological pump helps the ocean hold carbon away from the atmosphere, so a weaker pump could leave more carbon dioxide in the air. If widely used models are too simple, projections of future ocean carbon uptake may be too optimistic.
papers.limitations: This is a modelling study based on one Earth system model, so the results may not apply to other models. They have not been confirmed by direct observations.

key_terms.meaning: The set of processes by which marine life moves carbon from surface waters into the deep ocean.
The amount of organic carbon that sinks out of the sunlit surface layer into deeper water.
A computer simulation that couples the ocean, atmosphere, land and living systems to project climate.
The feeding links among small ocean organisms, such as algae and the tiny animals that graze on them.

papers.headline: Cutting carbon helps health and nature but may not ease resource demands
papers.original_title: Environmental and material implications of global climate mitigation pathways
papers.reason: Shows that deep decarbonization pathways benefit health and ecosystems but do not necessarily reduce land, water or mineral pressures.
papers.summary:
This study asks what happens to the environment and to raw materials when the world follows different routes to deep decarbonization, meaning large cuts in the greenhouse gases released by energy and industry. Beyond climate itself, the researchers looked at side effects such as human health, ecosystems, land use, water use and the mining of minerals and metals.

According to the short description available, deep decarbonization brings benefits for health and ecosystems. It does not automatically lower the pressure on land, water or minerals, though. The team also reports that different mitigation pathways change the timing of metal extraction, not the overall amount of metal needed.
papers.why_it_matters: Climate policy is often judged mainly by emissions, but a clean-energy transition still depends on land, water and mined metals. Knowing that pathways affect when metals are mined, rather than how much, can help planners prepare mining capacity and manage environmental impacts over time.
papers.limitations: Only a brief summary was available, so the methods, which pathways were compared, and the size of the effects are unclear. The work appears to rely on scenario modelling, which carries the uncertainties of its assumptions.

key_terms.meaning: Cutting carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gas emissions very sharply, typically toward near zero.
A scenario describing how energy systems, technologies and policies could change over time to limit climate change.
The strain created by demand for mined resources such as metals, including the environmental effects of extracting them.

papers.headline: Switching California homes from gas to electric pays off mainly where AC exists
papers.original_title: Exploring the distributional implications of targeted residential electrification in California
papers.reason: Data from 21,609 California homes show electrification economics vary widely, informing targeted incentives and rate reform for equitable adoption.
papers.summary:
Replacing gas furnaces, water heaters and stoves with electric versions is central to climate plans, but California's electricity is expensive, so it is unclear whether households come out ahead. The researchers used real smart-meter gas and electricity records from 21,609 randomly sampled single-family, gas-heated homes served by the utility PG&E in Northern and Central California. They estimated how much gas each home used for heating, hot water and cooking, converted that into the electricity heat pumps and induction stoves would need, and calculated each home's bills and net present value (NPV, whether lifetime savings outweigh upfront costs) under different electricity price structures, rebates and rollout orders.

Most homes saw small yearly bill savings (median under $156), but only about 15% came out ahead once equipment costs were counted, even on their best tariff. Homes that already had air conditioning did much better: when only switching space heating, 54–67% of them broke even, versus under 5% of homes without AC. Shifting more of the bill into fixed monthly charges, and federal income-based rebates, more than doubled the share of low- and moderate-income homes that broke even. Electrifying neighbourhoods with old gas pipes first cut emissions about as much as letting wealthier households go first and could avoid pipe replacement, but needed the largest subsidies. Full electrification also raised each home's peak demand modestly (7–17%) and created a second, winter peak on the grid.
papers.why_it_matters: Governments are spending money to move homes off gas, and this study shows which households are likely to gain and which need extra help. It also shows how electricity pricing and the order of rollout shape who bears costs as the gas network shrinks.
papers.limitations: This is a modelling study built on one utility's data from 2019, with assumptions about future prices, equipment costs, rebate eligibility and climate, and it excludes electric cars and fuels like propane; it is based on a preprint that had not been peer reviewed, so numbers in the final published paper may differ.

key_terms.meaning: The total of future savings minus costs over the equipment's life, with future money discounted; positive means the switch pays off.
An electric device that moves heat into or out of a home, providing both heating and cooling efficiently.
Volumetric charges depend on how much electricity you use; fixed charges are a set monthly fee regardless of use.
An electricity price that changes by time of day, higher during peak hours such as 4–9 PM.
The order in which groups of homes are converted, e.g. by income or by age of local gas pipes.

papers.headline: Thin air on the Tibetan Plateau stops Varroa mites from breeding
papers.original_title: Altitude-induced hypoxia suppresses Varroa mite reproduction in Tibetan honey bees
papers.reason: Translocation experiments indicate that altitude-induced hypoxia suppresses Varroa mite reproduction in Tibetan honey bee colonies.
papers.summary:
Varroa mites are tiny parasites that live on the outside of honey bees and are the most damaging pest beekeepers face, so most beekeepers must treat their hives with mite-killing chemicals again and again. Beekeepers on the Tibetan Plateau, however, say they hardly ever see these mites, which is unusual compared with the rest of China. The researchers wanted to understand why, so they moved bee colonies between locations in a series of relocation experiments.

They found that above about 3,500 metres, where the air holds less oxygen (a condition called hypoxia), female mites produced fewer offspring and their young stopped developing partway. Because of this, mite populations could not keep going over the long term. The team saw the same effects in colonies kept at low altitude but exposed to oxygen levels similar to those at 3,500 m, which points to low oxygen, rather than other features of high altitude, as the cause.
papers.why_it_matters: This reveals a previously unknown weakness of the Varroa mite: it seems unable to reproduce normally when oxygen is scarce. If this sensitivity can be exploited, it might lead to mite-control methods that do not rely on chemicals, helping beekeepers and supporting crop pollination and food supply.
papers.limitations: The authors note that the biological mechanism by which low oxygen blocks mite reproduction is still unknown and needs further study. It is also not yet shown whether low-oxygen treatment would be practical or safe for bees as a real-world control method.

key_terms.meaning: A parasitic mite that feeds on honey bees and their developing young; it is the biggest pest of managed honey bees worldwide.
A parasite that lives on the outside of its host's body rather than inside it.
A state of reduced oxygen availability, such as the thinner air found at high altitude.
How many offspring an animal produces.
A chemical pesticide used to kill mites.
A study in which organisms are moved from one place to another to test how the new environment affects them.

papers.headline: Tuning where acid sits inside hot-running fuel cells improves their output
papers.original_title: A membrane-guided strategy for optimizing proton exchange membrane fuel cells via spatially controlled acid distribution
papers.reason: A membrane-guided strategy controls phosphoric acid distribution to improve high-temperature proton exchange membrane fuel cells.
papers.summary:
High-temperature proton exchange membrane fuel cells use a polymer membrane soaked in phosphoric acid to carry protons (hydrogen ions) between electrodes. Some of this acid tends to move out of the membrane into the neighbouring catalyst layer, where platinum speeds up the electrode reactions. That shift has two sides. Acid in the catalyst layer helps protons reach the platinum, but the membrane is left with less acid and conducts protons less well. The researchers wanted to find out how much acid in the catalyst layer gives the best overall balance.

They made polybenzimidazole (PBI) membranes with extra side chains attached. These side chains offer many sites that bind acid. By changing the membranes, they could control how much acid each one absorbed and how strongly it held on to it. That in turn set how much acid leaked into the catalyst layer. To compare acid levels, they used the mass ratio of phosphorus to platinum in the catalyst layer as a rough measure. They then used an electrical analysis method to split the cell's losses into three parts: resistance, slow oxygen reactions, and difficulty moving oxygen to the catalyst. Under their test conditions, a phosphorus-to-platinum ratio of about 2 to 3 worked best. Their best membrane performed nearly twice as well as a standard PBI membrane called OPBI.
papers.why_it_matters: High-temperature fuel cells can tolerate impurities and simplify water and heat management, but acid loss and misplaced acid limit their performance. A simple measure of catalyst-layer acid, together with a target range, gives engineers a practical guide for designing membranes and electrodes.
papers.limitations: The best acid range applies only to the conditions tested, and the phosphorus-to-platinum ratio is described as a semiquantitative, approximate measure. The abstract gives no information on long-term durability.

key_terms.meaning: A device that turns hydrogen and oxygen into electricity, using a membrane that lets protons pass through but blocks electrons.
Soaking the polymer membrane in phosphoric acid so it can conduct protons at high temperatures without needing water.
A thin layer containing platinum particles where the fuel cell's chemical reactions happen.
A heat-resistant polymer commonly used as the membrane in high-temperature fuel cells; OPBI is one standard version of it.
A way of processing electrical impedance measurements to separate the different processes that cause energy losses in the cell.
The reaction at the cathode where oxygen gains electrons and combines with protons to form water.

papers.headline: Light-activated carbon dots made from plants target a major wheat fungus
papers.original_title: Plant-derived photocatalytic carbon dots for crop disease management
papers.reason: Plant-derived photocatalytic carbon dots offer a sustainable antifungal strategy against wheat Fusarium head blight.
papers.summary:
Fungi that attack crops cause large financial losses and threaten the world's food supply. One of the worst is Fusarium head blight, a fungal disease that infects the grain-bearing heads of wheat. The researchers wanted a new way to fight this disease.

Their approach uses carbon dots, which are extremely small carbon-based particles, made from plant material. These dots are photocatalytic, meaning they use light energy to drive chemical reactions. The short publisher description reports that this strategy works effectively against the fungus, but it does not explain how the dots harm the fungus, how they were tested, or how well they performed.
papers.why_it_matters: Wheat is a staple food for much of the world, so diseases that damage it put food security at risk. A treatment made from plant material and powered by light could offer another option for managing fungal crop diseases.
papers.limitations: The description is very brief. It does not say whether the method was tested in the lab, in greenhouses or in real fields, nor does it address cost, safety or effects on the environment.

key_terms.meaning: A destructive fungal disease of wheat that attacks the heads where the grain forms.
Tiny particles, only nanometres across, made mostly of carbon.
Able to use light to speed up or trigger a chemical reaction.
A fungus that causes disease in another organism, such as a crop plant.
